Allen vs. Costa
Arnold Allen, TKO, R4
Good bounce back fight for Allen. Costa is the more explosive and dangerous striker, with most of his KO wins coming from catching opponents as they close distance with kicks or counters. That said, I don’t think he has the cardio, pressure, or consistency to keep that threat going for a full 5 round fight, and he tends to fade badly in later rounds. Allen is more straightforward but more reliable, with better boxing, defense, and footwork that should help him avoid the worst of Costa’s kicking game. Neither fighter has a clear grappling advantage, so this is likely a mostly stand up fight where Allen’s durability and volume become more important over time. Overall, I think Allen shows levels. Costa is dangerous early, but Allen takes over late and can potentially finish the fight as Costa slows down.

Choi vs. Santos
Daniel Santos, TKO, R3
FOTN most likely. This is a close fight, but I’m leaning towards Santos. Choi is the more technical and polished striker, with better range control and cleaner shot selection, but he can struggle when forced into prolonged exchanges and high-pressure situations. And I don’t think his wins are very good. Santos brings nonstop pressure, high output, and a physical style that makes it hard for opponents to stay comfortable at range. He also has the ability to mix in takedowns, which could disrupt Choi’s rhythm and force him to defend more than he wants to. Even if Choi has early success picking shots from distance, I think Santos’s pace and physicality will start to break him down as the fight progresses. Choi tends to fade a bit in chaotic fights, especially when he’s getting hit consistently and forced backwards. Overall, I think Santos overwhelms him eventually and has a real chance to secure a finish in the later rounds once the damage and fatigue build up.

Wellmaker vs. Díaz
Malcolm Wellmaker, TKO, R1
My welding goat’s comeback. The Ewing loss doesn’t look that bad anymore and I don’t think Diaz is very dangerous despite the record, which is mostly built on weaker opposition. He’s primarily a volume striker, but he doesn’t have much power, can be hittable, and his boxing isn’t particularly clean or sharp. That said, Wellmaker is still a bit raw and somewhat one dimensional, relying heavily on big hooks and athleticism rather than a complete striking game. Diaz will likely try to keep this standing with higher output, but I think he’ll be more exposed to getting clipped because of his defensive flaws and lack of power. I lean Wellmaker because he’s the bigger, stronger puncher in a matchup where both guys are likely to strike in the pocket.

Bukauskas vs. Edwards
Modestas Bukauskas, TKO, R2
Should be a Lay-up. Let’s hope another Lithuanian doesn’t disappoint.

Cuamba vs. Sopaj
Benardo Sopaj, DEC
Low confidence even though I think Sopaj is the better fighter, the size difference kinda scared me. This is a strong main card fight and should be competitive. Cuamba is technical and skilled, but he fights too passively, doesn’t separate well in exchanges, and lacks real finishing power. Sopaj is more chaotic and dangerous, with heavy hands, high-intensity bursts, and the ability to hurt opponents even when he looks tired. Neither guy is likely to dominate grappling, but Sopaj is harder to hold down and more effective in scrambles, while Cuamba has shown issues on his back. I slightly favor Sopaj because his pressure and power give him more ways to win, maybe a potential late finish. 3x 29-28 Sopaj.

Veretennikov vs. Williams
Nikolay Veretennikov, DEC
Should be an ugly, entertaining brawl. Khaos’s game is very reliant on athleticism and power rather than clean technique, with poor fundamentals defensively and a lot of looping, messy striking. He can hurt people, but his recent performances are inconsistent. He’s looked outworked and outclassed at times when opponents close distance or match his pace. Veretennikov is also flawed and very hittable, but he’s more technical, uses a better jab and leg kicks, could even mix in takedowns of his own maybe, and can compete in the clinch with knees and pressure. I slightly favor Veretennikov because he’s more composed and less reliant on pure physical traits, while Khaos feels more like a KO or bust fighter.

Tokkos vs. Erslan
Ivan Erslan, TKO, R2
Cut whoever loses. Both of these guys feel barely UFC level, but I still lean Erslan. Tokkos has a style that completely falls apart if he can’t overwhelm opponents early with wrestling, and we’ve seen over and over that once the takedowns stop coming easily, his cardio, confidence, and striking all disappear with it. Erslan has his own flaws and isn’t UFC caliber either, but he’s shown enough toughness and scrambling ability against stronger competition to make me think he can survive the early pressure here. He may get taken down, but I don’t think he controls Erslan for 15 minutes. Erslan has more power, more willingness to fight through adversity, and a much clearer path to taking over  if Tokkos starts fading like he usually does. Plus he probably wants a UFC Belgrade fight.

Gantt vs. Minev
Tommy Gantt, SUB, R1
Gantt is a very legit prospect against a young debutant on short notice. Should be a fairly straightforward win for Gantt.

Vieira vs. Cavalcanti
Jacqueline Cavalcanti, DEC
This looks like another case of the UFC pushing a newer name against an established contender who may be declining. Viera has been near the top for years, but she’s always struggled with low output and a style that prioritizes control over damage, which has cost her in close decisions. Cavalcanti is still pretty unproven at this level, but her biggest strength is her striking. She's a clean, technical kickboxer who controls range well, mixes straight shots with kicks nicely, and rarely wastes movement, which could give Viera problems if this stays standing. That said, she hasn’t really faced anyone with Viera’s physical strength, grappling threat, or experience in long, grindy fights, so the takedown defense question is still a major factor. I still lean slightly toward Cavalcanti because of Viera’s declining pace and predictable approach, but it’s far from a confident pick.

Petroski vs. Brundage
Andre Petroski, DEC
Philly representative. This is a pretty low quality matchup and could be one of the worst fights of the year if it doesn’t end early. Brundage starts fast but fades quickly, and when things don’t go his way he usually looks for a way out, with inconsistent wins and frequent late fight collapses. Petroski is a slightly better overall grappler, but he’s also inconsistent and relies more on control than real finishing threat. Brundage does have a small early window on the feet with his explosiveness and occasional power, but that likely won’t hold up if he gets pressured or taken down. I expect Petroski to use wrestling and control to grind out a fairly straightforward win.

Ardelean vs. Viana
Alice Ardelean, DEC
Low level WMMA fight. I’m leaning Ardelean. She’s scrappy and has been in better recent form, even if her wins have come against very weak competition. Viana is dangerous in spots and has real finishing ability, but she’s extremely one dimensional on the ground and gives up takedowns and positions too easily. Ardelean’s best path is wrestling and pressure, and Viana has consistently struggled to defend or escape those situations.I think Ardelean’s activity and control are enough to edge a close fight against a very flawed opponent.

Barez vs. Gurule
Daniel Barez, DEC
50/50 fight and I'm gonna rock with the Spaniard. Barez is a skilled fighter with solid striking, even if he’s older, had a long layoff, and has issues once taken down. This is a very favorable matchup for him against Gurule, who hasn’t shown UFC level ability in any area so far. Gurule lacks power, doesn’t consistently put together effective offense, and often just moves without really winning exchanges. Barez has the cleaner, harder striking with straight punches and body kicks that should land consistently on Gurule’s open defense. Overall, I think Barez is the better, more dangerous fighter.

Bannon vs. Caliari
Nicolle Caliari, SUB, R2
Horrible WMMA fight. Bannon has had some UFC wins, but she has no grappling whatsoever and completely falls apart once she’s taken down. Caliari is also flawed, but she is aggressive, consistently tries to wrestle, push the pace, and find submissions. If she can get the fight to the ground, Bannon likely won’t have much to offer defensively. Caliari has the clearer path to winning through pressure and grappling.
